correct: Work in a group and tell your teacher where you will be digging.
Wear covered shoes and keep clear of the water's edge after rain.

wrong.text: Dig into the foot of a steep stream bank, because the clay is easiest to reach there.
wrong.why: The overhang can collapse on you. Dig only from open, stable ground.

wrong.text: Go alone to the riverbank to save time.
wrong.why: If the bank gives way or you slip, nobody can help. Stay with your group.

wrong.text: Start digging on a farm first, and explain to the owner afterwards.
wrong.why: Permission comes first, from the landowner or community.

wrong.text: Eat your groundnuts straight after handling the samples, as clay is only earth.
wrong.why: Soil can carry germs and worms. Wash your hands first.

wrong.text: Leave your pit open and unmarked when you go.
wrong.why: People and animals can fall in. Fill it in or make it safe.

wrong.text: Swing the hoe while a friend scoops clay out of the same hole.
wrong.why: The hoe can strike your friend. Take turns, and stand clear.

distractors.name: Potter's wheel
distractors.why: Forming comes much later. This job only finds and tests clay.

distractors.name: Rolling pin
distractors.why: Field tests are done by hand with a pinch and a coil.

distractors.name: Glaze brush
distractors.why: Nothing is glazed at the survey stage.

distractors.name: Serrated kidney
distractors.why: It scrapes pot walls. No pot is made here.

distractors.name: Plaster bat
distractors.why: Bats dry prepared slip. This sample is only weighed and dried.

distractors.name: Sieve
distractors.why: Sieving is part of preparing clay, not of the field survey.

decisions.prompt: You have started digging. The top layer is dark and full of roots. What do you do?

options.text: Remove it and dig down to the clay layer
options.consequence: Your sample is true clay, with no organic matter in it.

options.text: Bag some now, because it is the easiest to reach and it is soft and moist too
options.consequence: That is topsoil, not clay. It is one of the commonest mistakes here.

options.text: Mix it into the clay to give a bigger sample
options.consequence: Organic matter spoils the sample, and the layers can no longer be told apart.

decisions.prompt: You have dug through a grey layer into a red layer. How do you sample them?

options.text: Bag each layer alone, with its depth on the label
options.consequence: Each result belongs to one clay, so you can compare them later.

options.text: Mix them, as that gives an average of the site
options.consequence: Mixed layers hide what each clay is like, which is a source of error.

options.text: Keep only the prettier colour and record nothing about the other layer
options.consequence: The record of the deposit is now incomplete.

decisions.prompt: The rain is coming and you have three bags to fill. When do you label them?

options.text: Now, as each bag is filled
options.consequence: No sample can be mixed up with another.

options.text: Back at school, when your hands are clean and you can write neatly
options.consequence: You may no longer remember which bag came from which depth.

options.text: Only the first, as the rest came from the same area
options.consequence: Site, depth and date must be on each bag.

decisions.prompt: Your clay has dried overnight. How do you know it is fully dry?

options.text: Weigh, dry further, and weigh until the mass stops falling
options.consequence: Constant mass shows all the free water has gone.

options.text: It looks pale and feels dry, so record that mass
options.consequence: Clay can look dry and still hold water, so the result comes out low.

options.text: Dry it for the same time as last year's class did
options.consequence: Drying time varies. Only constant mass proves it is dry.

observations.prompt: You bend a 1 cm coil round your finger and it bends with no cracks. What does this show?

options.text: Good plasticity
Too much sand
options.why: Sandy clays crack and feel gritty.

options.text: It is a white primary clay
The clay is too dry to use

observations.prompt: A white clay from a site where it formed has low plasticity. What is it most likely to be?

options.text: A primary clay such as kaolin
A secondary ball clay
A red earthenware clay
options.why: That is a coloured, plastic secondary clay.

options.text: Sand
options.why: Sand is gritty and has no plasticity.

numerics.prompt: A clay sample weighs 250 g wet and {d} g dry. What is its water content on a dry basis?
A sample weighs 250 g wet and {d} g dry. What is its water content on a wet basis?

faults.scenario: Emeka's prospecting report gave a strange water content. Here is what he did.

lines.text: He did not say whether his water content was on a wet or dry basis.
lines.why: The two give different numbers. State which one you used.

lines.text: He left his open bags in the sun for two days before weighing the wet clay.
lines.why: The sample dried out before it was weighed, so the wet mass is too low.

lines.text: He bagged several layers together.
lines.why: Mixed layers are a source of error.

lines.text: He asked the community for permission to dig.
He recorded the depth, colour and thickness of the layer.

written.precautionsPrompt: State two precautions for sampling clay and finding its water content.
written.explainPrompt: Why must you state whether water content is on a wet or dry basis?
written.explainGuide: The same water is divided by a different mass. The dry basis divides by the dry mass and the wet basis by the wet mass, so the percentages differ. For 250 g wet and 200 g dry, they are 25% and 20%.

board: Ask first. Keep clear of high banks

correct: Let only your teacher load, fire and unload the kiln.
Damp-wipe the bench so that dry clay dust does not build up.

wrong.text: Open the kiln door a little to see how the bars are doing.
wrong.why: A hot kiln can burn you, and the cold air can crack the ware. Never open it hot.

wrong.text: Lift the warm bars out with a dry rag, because they are not glowing any more.
wrong.why: They can be hot enough to burn you badly. Wait until the kiln has cooled.

wrong.text: Stand and lean on the kiln to read the temperature during firing.
wrong.why: The case is hot. Keep clear unless the teacher directs you.

wrong.text: Sweep dry clay crumbs off the bench with your hand.
wrong.why: This raises silica dust. Wipe with a damp cloth.

wrong.text: Put a damp bar into the kiln to save time.
wrong.why: Steam can burst it, and it can damage other work. It must be fully dry.

distractors.name: Potter's wheel
distractors.why: The test uses flat bars cut from a slab.

distractors.name: Plaster mould
distractors.why: The bars are cut with a knife and ruler.

distractors.name: Banding wheel
distractors.why: There is nothing to turn in this test.

distractors.name: Glaze
distractors.why: A bare bar shows the true shrinkage of the clay.

distractors.name: Spring balance
distractors.why: The test measures length, not mass.

distractors.name: Wooden school ruler with worn ends
distractors.why: It cannot be read closely enough. Use the calliper or steel rule.

decisions.prompt: You are about to scratch the 10.0 cm line. How do you mark it?

options.text: Two fine, sharp marks set exactly 10.0 cm apart
options.consequence: Each later reading is from the same exact points.

options.text: Two broad marks that are easy to see from a distance
options.consequence: Broad marks leave you unsure where to read, so the result is rough.

options.text: One long groove pressed deep to the bottom of the bar
options.consequence: A deep groove weakens the bar, and it can crack along the line.

decisions.prompt: The bars need to dry by tomorrow. Where do you put them?

options.text: In a sheltered place, turning them often
options.consequence: They dry slowly and evenly, and stay flat for measuring.

options.text: In strong sun on one side, to speed them up
options.consequence: One side shrinks faster, so the bars warp and the lengths are false.

options.text: On top of the warm kiln with no turning
options.consequence: Fast one-sided drying warps them and can crack them.

decisions.prompt: You are working out firing shrinkage. Which length do you divide by?

options.text: The dry length
options.consequence: Firing starts from the dry bar, so that is the base.

options.text: The plastic length of 10.0 cm
options.consequence: That is the common mistake. It gives a lower, wrong figure.

options.text: The fired length
options.consequence: Shrinkage is worked out on the size before the change.

decisions.prompt: Your three bars give 11%, 10.8% and 11.2%. What do you report?

options.text: The mean of the three bars
options.consequence: Averaging evens out small errors between bars.

options.text: The highest, to be on the safe side
options.consequence: One bar does not represent the clay.

options.text: Only the bar that looks best
options.consequence: Dropping results without a reason is poor practice.

observations.prompt: What happens to the 10.0 cm line through the test?

options.text: It gets shorter after drying, then shorter again after firing
It gets shorter on drying, then returns to 10.0 cm on firing
options.why: Fired clay does not expand back.

options.text: It stays 10.0 cm until the bar is fired
options.why: Water loss on drying shrinks it first.

options.text: It gets longer after firing

observations.prompt: Clay A is fine and plastic. Clay B has grog in it. Which shrinks more?

options.text: Clay A
Clay B
options.why: Grog opens the body and reduces shrinkage.

options.text: They shrink exactly the same
Neither shrinks

numerics.prompt: A 10.0 cm line measures {d} cm when dry. What is the drying shrinkage?
A 10.0 cm line measures {f} cm when fired. What is the total shrinkage?
A line measures {d} cm dry and {f} cm fired. What is the firing shrinkage, worked on the dry length?

faults.scenario: Tunde's fired pots came out smaller than planned, and his report was marked down. Here is what he did.

lines.text: He added the shrinkage percentage to the finished size.
lines.why: The wet size is the finished size divided by (1 − shrinkage).

lines.text: He worked out firing shrinkage on the plastic length.
lines.why: It must be worked on the dry length.

lines.text: He measured a warped bar along its bend.
He labelled each bar.
He averaged his three bars.
lines.why: Using the mean is the right way to report the result.

written.precautionsPrompt: State two precautions for an accurate shrinkage test.
written.explainPrompt: Why do you divide by (1 − shrinkage) to find the wet size, and not simply add the percentage?
written.explainGuide: The percentage is a share of the wet size, not of the fired size. The fired size equals wet size × (1 − shrinkage), so the wet size is the fired size ÷ (1 − shrinkage). Adding the percentage gives a pot that is too small.

correct: Keep the wedging table clean with a damp sponge after use.
Mop up spilled slip at once, as a wet floor is slippery.

wrong.text: Sweep up dry clay dust with a broom at the end of the lesson.
wrong.why: This puts silica dust in the air you breathe. Damp-mop instead.

wrong.text: Crush dry lumps without a mask because the job only takes a minute.
wrong.why: Silica dust harms the lungs. Wear a dust mask.

wrong.text: Lift a full slip bucket by bending your back.
wrong.why: You can injure your back. Bend your knees, keep your back straight, or share the load.

wrong.text: Pour slip waste down the sink.
wrong.why: Clay sets in pipes and blocks them. Let it settle and reuse it.

wrong.text: Pull the cutting wire towards your body with both hands.
wrong.why: The wire can snap through and cut you. Pull it down through the clay, away from you.

wrong.text: Leave a bucket of slip in the walkway.
wrong.why: People trip over it. Keep buckets by the wall.

distractors.why: Forming comes after the clay is ready.

distractors.why: Nothing has been thrown yet.

distractors.name: Cottle boards
distractors.why: They hold plaster for moulds.

distractors.name: Fine paint brush
distractors.why: Nothing here is painted.

decisions.prompt: The slip is ready, but the sieve is slow and the class is waiting. What do you do?

options.text: Keep sieving until it has all passed through
options.consequence: Stones and roots are out, so there will be no blow-outs in the kiln.

options.text: Skip sieving, since a few small stones never hurt a pot and the class is waiting
options.consequence: Stones cause blow-outs in the kiln.

options.text: Pour it through a coarse basket instead
options.consequence: Sand and small stones go through, and they stay in the body.

decisions.prompt: Your slip on the plaster bats has reached a soft plastic stage. What do you do?

options.text: Take it off now, before it dries too hard
options.consequence: The clay is ready to wedge without lumps.

options.text: Leave it for a day longer to be sure
options.consequence: It dries too hard, so it forms lumps and must be slaked again.

options.text: Add more slip on top of it
options.consequence: The layers dry unevenly and form lumps.

decisions.prompt: You must blend in 10% grog. How do you measure it?

options.text: Weigh the clay and the grog
options.consequence: The blend is exact and can be repeated.

options.text: Add a few handfuls and judge by feel
options.consequence: You cannot repeat it, and the shrinkage will change.

options.text: Measure it by the height of the bucket
options.consequence: Volume in a bucket does not give the proportion by weight.

decisions.prompt: You cut the wedged clay and see small holes in the cut faces. What do you do?

options.text: Keep wedging and cut again until the holes are gone
options.consequence: The clay is free of air, so the ware will not burst in the kiln.

options.text: Go ahead, since the air will escape as it dries
options.consequence: Trapped air stays there and can burst the ware in the kiln.

options.text: Smooth the holes over with a wet finger
options.consequence: This covers the surface. The air inside remains.

observations.prompt: You cut a well-wedged ball with the wire. What do the cut faces look like?

options.text: Smooth, one colour, with no air holes
Marbled with streaks
options.why: Streaks show that blending is not finished.

options.text: Full of small pockets
Dry and crumbling
options.why: That clay is too dry to wedge.

observations.prompt: Why does sieving matter for fired work?

options.text: Stones left in the clay can cause blow-outs in the kiln
Stones turn the clay red when it is fired
options.why: Colour depends on iron content, not on stones.

options.text: Sieving makes the clay shrink less in firing
options.why: Sieving removes debris. Grog is what reduces shrinkage.

options.text: Sieved clay needs no wedging afterwards

numerics.prompt: Blend {a} parts plastic clay with 1 part kaolin to make {t} kg. How much plastic clay do you need?

You add grog at {p}% of {m} kg of clay. How much grog do you add?

faults.scenario: Bisi's pots burst in the kiln. Here is what she did.

lines.text: She skipped the sieve, so stones stayed in the clay.
She folded the clay over carelessly as she wedged it.
She stopped wedging without cutting the clay to check it.
lines.why: Cut faces must show no air holes or streaks.

written.precautionsPrompt: State two precautions for preparing a good clay body.
written.explainPrompt: Why must air be removed from clay before it is formed and fired?
written.explainGuide: Trapped air expands in the kiln and can burst the ware. Air pockets also make the clay uneven to form. Wedging removes the air and makes the clay uniform.

correct: Wipe the bench with a damp sponge at the end of the lesson.
Hold the needle tool with its point down and pass it handle first.

wrong.text: Brush dry clay off your overall with your hands.
wrong.why: This raises dust. Change, or wipe it down damp.

wrong.text: Leave the hacksaw blade on the edge of the bench, teeth outwards.
wrong.why: It cuts anyone who reaches past. Store it away safely.

wrong.text: Eat at the bench without washing the clay off your hands.
wrong.why: Clay and slip do not belong in your food. Wash first.

wrong.text: Blow dry dust off the finished rim.
wrong.why: Silica dust goes into your lungs and eyes. Sponge the rim.

wrong.text: Tip dirty slip water into the sink.
wrong.why: Clay blocks the drains. Let it settle and reuse the sediment.

decisions.prompt: You are about to lay the first coil on the base. What do you do?

options.text: Score both surfaces and apply slip
options.consequence: The joint holds firm when dry.

options.text: Press it on firmly, as wet clay sticks to itself and there is no need for any more
options.consequence: Unscored joints crack on drying.

options.text: Wet it with plain water only
options.consequence: Water alone does not make a firm bond.

decisions.prompt: The coils are in place. What do you do with the inside joints?

options.text: Blend each one with your finger or a tool
options.consequence: The wall becomes one piece, so it will not split along the coils.

options.text: Leave them, as they will not be seen inside
options.consequence: Unblended joints are weak and split apart.

options.text: Fill the gaps with dry clay powder
options.consequence: Powder does not bond, and the join remains weak.

decisions.prompt: The vase is getting soft and sagging after several coils. What do you do?

options.text: Stop, and let the lower coils stiffen a little
options.consequence: The base firms up and can take more weight.

options.text: Add more coils quickly before it moves further
options.consequence: Building too fast makes the form collapse.

options.text: Wrap the outside in dry newspaper and carry on building
options.consequence: The soft wall still has to take the weight.

decisions.prompt: You must stop until tomorrow. What do you do with the pot?

options.text: Cover it with polythene
options.consequence: The clay stays workable, so the next coil will join.

options.text: Leave it uncovered so that it firms up well by morning
options.consequence: It dries too far, and new coils will crack away.

options.text: Soak it in water so it stays soft
options.consequence: It collapses, because it cannot take water.

observations.prompt: Which joint can you expect to crack as the pot dries?

options.text: One made with no scoring or slip
One scored and slipped, then blended
options.why: That is the correct way to join.

options.text: One blended well on the inside
One covered with polythene

written.precautionsPrompt: State two precautions for building an even coil vase.
written.explainPrompt: Why is every join scored and slipped in hand building?
written.explainGuide: Scoring roughens the two surfaces and slip acts as a glue of clay. The two parts key together and shrink as one, so the join does not crack on drying.

board: Check the profile against the template

correct: Cut on the board with the blade moving away from your hand.

wrong.text: Leave the knife under the slab.
wrong.why: The next person who lifts the slab will be cut. Keep it in view.

decisions.prompt: You want to build the box walls. How firm should the slab be?

options.text: Leather-hard

options.consequence: The soft slab distorts, and the join still cracks.

options.why: Soft clay bends. It does not crack.

options.text: It shrinks to half its size

written.explainGuide: Leather-hard clay is firm enough to stand and give crisp edges, but still moist enough to be scored, slipped and joined. Both parts then shrink together, so the joints do not crack.

correct: Check that the wheel head is clear before you switch on.

options.consequence: There is enough clay for the base and the foot.

decisions.prompt: Water has collected in the bottom of the pot. What do you do?

options.text: Sponge it out with the sponge on a stick
options.consequence: The base does not soften or crack.

options.consequence: The soaked base weakens and may crack.

options.consequence: This spoils the pot, and it can throw it off.

decisions.prompt: The wall is getting wet and floppy halfway up. What do you do?

options.consequence: The wall stays strong and rises evenly.

options.text: Add more water and pull faster to finish
options.consequence: Too much water and speed make the wall collapse.

options.text: Press hard at the rim only
options.consequence: The thick lower wall stays, and the rim may tear.

decisions.prompt: You will trim the foot. When?

options.text: At leather-hard, upside down and re-centred
options.consequence: The clay cuts cleanly, and the pot keeps its shape.

options.text: Straight away while it is still wet on the wheel head
options.consequence: Wet clay smears and distorts.

options.text: When bone dry

written.precautionsPrompt: State two precautions for making hand tools from wood and metal.
written.explainPrompt: Why should finished tools be sanded and then oiled or waxed?
written.explainGuide: Sanding removes splinters and rough spots that would hurt your hands or tear the clay. Oil or wax seals the wood, and oil stops metal parts rusting.

correct: Lay the compasses flat and closed when you are not using them.
Work in good light, sitting upright.

wrong.text: Cut the card template while holding it against your hand.
wrong.why: The blade can go through into your hand. Cut on a board.

wrong.text: Leave the compass open on your chair.
wrong.why: Someone can sit on it.

wrong.text: Sharpen your pencil with a loose razor blade.
wrong.why: Loose blades cut fingers. Use a sharpener.

wrong.text: Lean close to the paper in poor light for hours.
wrong.why: It strains your eyes and back.

wrong.text: Throw a set square to a friend.
wrong.why: Its corners can injure. Hand it over.

written.precautionsPrompt: State two precautions for a good working drawing.
written.explainPrompt: Why does a working drawing give both fired and wet dimensions?
written.explainGuide: The clay shrinks in drying and firing, so the pot has to be made larger than the size required. The wet size is the fired size divided by (1 − shrinkage).

decisions.prompt: You made 20 vases, but 2 cracked in the firing. What do you divide the total by?

options.text: 18, the number of saleable wares

options.text: 20, the number that you made
options.consequence: You sell only 18, so you lose money.

options.text: 22, to add a safety margin

options.text: Add it only if there is a profit

options.text: Halve it to sell out quickly

written.precautionsPrompt: State two precautions for costing a batch of ceramic ware.
written.explainPrompt: Why is the total cost divided by the number of good wares and not by the number made?
written.explainGuide: Only the good wares can be sold, so they must recover all the money spent, including the cost of the wares that were lost in firing.
